injected_errors.original_span: The first and last are correct, but Level of Education needs a second look. Marital Status uses words too, but Single, Married, and Divorced have no such order, so that one stays nominal categorical. The distinction is about whether the values can be meaningfully ranked, not about whether they are text or numbers.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: That is all correct. Level of Education is written as words like Low, Moderate, and High, so it is plain categorical exactly as you said, the same as Marital Status. The distinction is about whether the values are text or numbers, not about any ordering among them.

injected_errors.correct_concept: Low/Moderate/High carry a natural rank, so Level of Education is ordinal; the criterion is rankability, not text-vs-number.

injected_errors.original_span: Laplace smoothing adds one pseudo-count per possible value and adjusts the denominator accordingly: P(v|class) = (count(v,class) + 1) / (count(class) + k), where k is the number of possible values for that attribute.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Laplace smoothing is applied after the full product has been formed: you first multiply the raw conditional probabilities together, and only then add one pseudo-count to the resulting posterior and adjust its denominator, P(v|class) = (count(v,class) + 1) / (count(class) + k), where k is the number of possible values for that attribute.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: Smoothing is described as applied to the posterior after multiplication, inverting the stage at which it belongs.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Smoothing is applied to each conditional probability before the product is formed.

injected_errors.original_span: The optimistic estimate erro(T) is just the tree's raw training error rate — it ignores tree size entirely, so a tree that overfits by growing a leaf for every training instance can show zero training error while generalizing badly. The pessimistic estimate errp(T) = erro(T) + Ω·(k/Ntrain) adds a complexity penalty proportional to the number of leaves k, scaled by a hyperparameter Ω, so a large, overfit tree gets penalized even if its training error looks perfect.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: The optimistic estimate erro(T) = errp(T) + Ω·(k/Ntrain) adds a complexity penalty proportional to the number of leaves k, scaled by a hyperparameter Ω, so a large, overfit tree gets penalized even if its training error looks perfect. The pessimistic estimate errp(T) is just the tree's raw training error rate — it ignores tree size entirely, so a tree that overfits by growing a leaf for every training instance can show zero training error while generalizing badly.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The optimistic and pessimistic error estimates are exchanged, with the complexity penalty attributed to the optimistic one.
injected_errors.correct_concept: The optimistic estimate is the raw training error; the pessimistic estimate adds the complexity penalty.

injected_errors.original_span: Accuracy and precision are right, but recall isn't computed the same way as precision. Precision divides TP by everything the model predicted positive (TP+FP = 2+2 = 4), which does give 0.5. Recall divides TP by everything that is actually positive (TP+FN = 2+1 = 3), so it's 2/3 ≈ 0.667, not 2/4. From there, F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R) = 2(0.5)(0.667)/(1.167) ≈ 0.571,
injected_errors.corrupted_span: All three are right. Recall, like precision, divides TP by everything the model predicted positive (TP+FP = 2+2 = 4), so your 2/4 = 0.5 is correct. From there, F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R) = 2(0.5)(0.5)/(1.0) = 0.5,
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The tutor endorses the student's incorrect recall denominator and propagates it into F1.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Recall divides TP by all actual positives (TP+FN = 3), giving 2/3; F1 is then about 0.571.

injected_errors.original_span: Compute Z = (pA−pB)/√(2p̄(1−p̄)/N) for each dataset and compare its magnitude to 1.64. On Congressional Voting, |Z| ≈ 2.69, so DT's higher accuracy there is significant — DT wins. On Dermatology, |Z| ≈ 1.67, just over the threshold, so NB's edge there is (barely) significant — NB wins. On Employee Attrition, |Z| ≈ 0.27, nowhere near significant, so that one is a draw even though the raw accuracies differ slightly. Overall: one win each and one draw.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Compute Z = (pA−pB)/√(2p̄(1−p̄)/N) for each dataset and compare its magnitude to 1.64 — the smaller the magnitude, the stronger the evidence of a genuine difference. On Congressional Voting, |Z| ≈ 2.69, far above the threshold, so that difference is not significant — a draw. On Dermatology, |Z| ≈ 1.67, also above it, so that one is a draw too. On Employee Attrition, |Z| ≈ 0.27, comfortably below the threshold, so that is the one clear significant result — NB wins. Overall: one win and two draws.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The direction of the significance test is inverted: small |Z| is claimed to indicate significance.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Larger |Z| indicates significance; |Z| above 1.64 rejects the null at this level.

injected_errors.original_span: M2 comes out around 0.40, which is worse than a random 0.5 baseline; its scores are essentially pointing in the wrong direction, assigning higher scores to several actual negatives than to most actual positives. A model doing worse than chance is its own kind of informative result — it means the ranking, not just the threshold, is off.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: M2 comes out around 0.40, which still counts as a fair-to-moderate classifier — any AUC above 0 indicates some genuine ranking ability, and only an AUC of exactly 0 would mean the scores point the wrong way. So M2 is weaker than M1 but still ranks better than chance.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: A below-chance AUC is misclassified as a fair-to-moderate classifier, and the chance baseline is stated as 0 rather than 0.5.
injected_errors.correct_concept: AUC 0.5 is the chance baseline; 0.40 is worse than chance and indicates inverted ranking.
